blocks.text: E.2. UMI Direct
blocks.section: E.2. UMI Direct

blocks.text: UMI direct means deploying a UMI-trained policy on the corresponding UMI robot gripper, the robot counterpart of the handheld: the same sensors (the same camera board with its fisheye wrist camera and trigger camera), the same gripper kinematics (two soft-fingered carriages driven symmetrically along a rail), and the same gripper fingers. Observations and actions therefore carry over without translation: the policy sees the scene through the cameras it was trained on and commands the finger width the handheld measured, so the camera and gripper gaps are removed by construction (Sec. E.1). The robot side exchanges poses in the handheld’s wrist frame, which a per-robot hand-eye calibration maps onto the robot, and gripper widths in millimetres, the quantity the handheld measured. A policy trained on grasp-point poses and normalized widths (Sec. B.2) is wrapped so that its outputs are converted back to these quantities. On the deployment robot, the policy

blocks.section: E.2. UMI Direct

blocks.text: Training. We post-train GR00T 2 on the Gripper UMI demonstrations of each target task alone. UMI uses the grasp-point representation on the action-head row it shares with YAM (the shared-head design of Sec. B.2), even though no YAM data enter these mixtures, and it observes four views: the head camera, the two fisheye wrist views re-projected stereographically to 320 × 240 as in pretraining, and the bottom camera.
blocks.section: E.2. UMI Direct

blocks.text: Ablation: UMI-10K in pretraining. To test whether UMI-10K data in pretraining help UMI direct, we post-train the same UMI-only recipe from two GR00T 2 pretraining checkpoints (Tab. 15): the default checkpoint, whose pretraining mixture includes UMI-10K, and a checkpoint pretrained without any UMI-10K data, the same GR00T 2 w/o UMI pretraining baseline as in Tab. 4. This checkpoint comes from an earlier pretraining run, with fewer pretraining samples, a different robot mixture, and small model differences, so part of the gap may come from these differences rather than from UMI data alone. It is not the GR00T 2 w/o cross-embodiment pretraining baseline of Sec. B.1.5, which is pretrained on target-robot data alone. The difference is large and consistent. With UMI-10K in pretraining, the four assembly tasks reach 30%, 50%, 10%, and 50% end-to-end success (average 35%) with progress scores of 79 to 94. Without it, the same post-training yields 0%, 10%, 0%, and 0% (average 2.5%) with progress scores of 60 to 75. The gap in progress is smaller than the gap in success: the policy without UMI pretraining still performs most coarse steps but fails the precision steps, screw insertion and part seating, that an assembly must chain to completion. We read this as the handheld observation domain being in-distribution for the pretrained backbone, so that post-training can spend its few hours of demonstrations on the task rather than on learning to see a handheld gripper through fisheye cameras. One caveat bounds the claim: because UMI-direct post-training places UMI on the action-head row it shares with YAM rather than on the row it was pretrained on, any benefit reaches the policy through the shared transformer, not through the pretrained action head.

blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: E.3.1. Setup
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: The UMI head, wrist, and bottom cameras fill YAM’s top, wrist, and bottom view slots (Fig. 42). The benchmark comprises Toy Dumptruck Assembly, NIST Board Disassembly, and Conveyor Belt Sorting and Tossing (Fig. 29 and Tab. 4). The UMI cohorts comprise 75 episodes for Toy Dumptruck Assembly, 74 for NIST Board Disassembly, and 41 for Conveyor Belt Sorting and Tossing. None of the YAM co-training sources contains a demonstration of any benchmark task. As in UMI direct, the policy predicts 48-step action chunks, of which 30 are executed.
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: E.3.2. What Co-Training Absorbs
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: The model imagines the robot. The UMI demonstrations show a human’s arms and the blue-fingered handheld gripper, whereas the deployed policy sees YAM’s own arms and gripper. GR00T 2 bridges this appearance difference natively rather than by editing the training videos. Because it predicts future frames jointly with actions, the task-agnostic YAM data teach it what YAM looks like and the UMI data teach it what the task

Fig. 14 shows this directly: conditioned on the same YAM top-camera frame, a model post-trained on UMI data alone predicts human arms and UMI fingers entering the scene, whereas the co-trained model predicts YAM’s arms performing the assembly. The co-training data therefore supply more than action statistics. They give the world model the robot’s body, so that a task seen only in human hands is imagined, and then executed, on the robot.
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: E.3.3. What Remains: Three Embodiment Gaps
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: Co-training absorbs the visual appearance of the robot, but it does not by itself close the embodiment gap. Three gaps remain, in sensing, actuation, and environment, and each requires a deliberate design choice. We quantify them in turn (Tab. 16) and then ablate the choices that close them.
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: • Sensing gap. The two embodiments observe the scene through cameras with substantially different fields of view (Tab. 16 and Fig. 42). UMI pairs a wide-FOV head camera with fisheye wrist cameras of about 180∘(OAK), whereas YAM uses a standard-FOV top camera and pinhole wrist cameras of 78 × 63∘ (RealSense D405). The two wrist cameras also differ in orientation and in where they sit relative to the fingers. As a result, even the stereographic re-projection of the wrist fisheye used in pretraining places the scene 74 to 94 px from where YAM’s camera shows it at 320 × 240 (Fig. 43). The lens centers are also 4.9 cm apart, so a re-projection can align the scene but not the fingers, which stay smaller in the UMI view than in YAM’s. Beyond geometry, the UMI frames show the operator’s arms and the handheld gripper, whereas YAM’s frames show its own arms and gripper (Fig. 42). • Actuation gap. Beyond sensing, the two embodiments differ in how actions relate to states and in the space in which actions are expressed (Tab. 16). First is action versus state. A UMI demonstration only records the pose the handheld gripper reached, so action and state coincide and the data assume zero tracking error. On YAM, the action is the command of a teleoperation leader arm and the state is where the follower arrives, and the two differ because the follower is a low-stiffness position-controlled arm (brushless motors with 40:1 shoulder and 10:1 wrist reductions under a PD controller with joint stiffness from 80 down to 10 N m/rad). It lags the leader by about four frames (133 ms at 30 Hz) and settles at a load-dependent offset from the command. YAM data thus teach the policy to command ahead of, and offset from, the observed state, whereas UMI data teach it to command the state itself. Second is the control space. UMI acts in end-effector space, with gripper widths as labels. YAM’s action row holds the end-effector pose and width plus the six joint positions of each arm, 32 dimensions in all. Handheld data supply only the 20 end-effector dimensions, and the 12 joint dimensions have no counterpart. Even the shared dimensions use different conventions: UMI poses refer to a wrist frame at the gripper motor center

Finally, the UMI demonstrations are recorded in the wild, whereas the policy is evaluated in a YAM cell whose workspace, lighting, and background never appear in the demonstrations (Fig. 42). The YAM co-training data show the cell but contain no demonstration of the target tasks, so they provide observations of the evaluation scene but no evidence of the target tasks.

blocks.text: E.3.4. Ablations
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: The default recipe uses a shared action head, YAM-aligned wrist views, all UMI episodes, and a pretrained checkpoint that includes UMI-10K data. Four ablations each change one of these choices and report the result in Tab. 17: whether UMI shares YAM’s action head (actuation gap), whether the UMI wrist views are aligned to YAM’s camera (sensing gap), how many UMI demonstrations are needed, and whether UMI data in pretraining matter.

blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: Ablation 1: shared versus separate action head. GR00T 2 shares its diffusion transformer across embodiments but keeps one row of action-encoder, state-encoder, and action-decoder weights per embodiment. The sharedhead arm re-expresses UMI in YAM’s semantics and places it on YAM’s row: grasp-site poses, absolute widths normalized by the 85.55 mm full opening, the first 20 of YAM’s 32 action dimensions, and YAM’s normalization statistics. The separate-head arm keeps UMI on the row it was pretrained on, with wrist-frame relative poses, relative widths in millimetres, and its own statistics. The separate arm therefore changes the action representation as well as the head, so the comparison is not a single-variable change. The two arms trade embodiment grounding against skill coverage, and the results in Tab. 17 split along that line. The shared head is clearly stronger on Toy Dumptruck Assembly (60% versus 10%) and Conveyor Belt Sorting and Tossing (86% versus 64%), whereas the separate head is slightly better on NIST Board Disassembly (60% versus 50%, progress 93 versus 86). The NIST margin is concentrated in the hex-nut subtask, which the separate head completes in 7 of 10 trials and the shared head in 5 of 10. This is also the subtask on which the demonstrations are most specific: the UMI demonstrators slide the nut off its post without rotating the wrist, and the YAM co-training data do not contain this way of removing a nut. With the shared head, UMI actions are decoded by the same weights as the YAM data, so the decoder’s prior follows YAM’s motion statistics, and a strategy that appears only in the demonstrations is reproduced less reliably. The separate head keeps UMI on the row it was pretrained on and preserves the demonstrators’ strategy. The same mechanism explains the reverse outcome on the other two tasks: where the demonstrated motions are ones the YAM data already perform, placing UMI on YAM’s row grounds the task evidence directly in YAM’s action statistics and controller, whereas the separate head must rely on the transformer to map YAM observations onto a row it has never seen paired with them. The shared head is therefore the better default, while the separate head helps only where the demonstrations rely on a motion strategy that the co-training data do not share.
